nodes.heading: Family Violence Protection Act 2008
nodes.text: Family Violence Protection Act 2008

nodes.heading: Preliminary
nodes.text: Authorised Version incorporating amendments as at 26 April 2026 Preamble In enacting this Act, the Parliament recognises the following principles—
that non-violence is a fundamental social value that must be promoted;
that family violence is a fundamental violation of human rights and is unacceptable in any form;
that family violence is not acceptable in any community or culture;
that, in responding to family violence and promoting the safety of persons who have experienced family violence, the justice system should treat the views of victims of family violence with respect.
In enacting this Act, the Parliament also recognises the following features of family violence—
that while anyone can be a victim or perpetrator of family violence, family violence is predominantly committed by men against women, children and other vulnerable persons;

that children who are exposed to the effects of family violence are particularly vulnerable and exposure to family violence may have a serious impact on children's current and future physical, psychological and emotional wellbeing;
that family violence—
affects the entire community; and
occurs in all areas of society, regardless of location, socioeconomic and health status, age, culture, gender, sexual identity, ability, ethnicity or religion;
that family violence extends beyond physical and sexual violence and may involve emotional or psychological abuse and economic abuse;
that family violence may involve overt or subtle exploitation of power imbalances and may consist of isolated incidents or patterns of abuse over a period of time.

nodes.heading: Purpose
nodes.text: The purpose of this Act is to—
maximise safety for children and adults who have experienced family violence; and
prevent and reduce family violence to the greatest extent possible; and
promote the accountability of perpetrators of family violence for their actions.

nodes.heading: How purpose is to be achieved
nodes.text: This Act aims to achieve its purpose by—
providing an effective and accessible system of family violence intervention orders and family violence safety notices; and
providing for the sharing of information that is relevant to assessing and managing a risk of family violence; and
creating offences for contraventions of family violence intervention orders and family violence safety notices; and
providing a framework for achieving consistency in family violence risk assessment and family violence risk management.

nodes.text: For the purposes of this Act, family violence is—
behaviour by a person towards a family member of that person if that behaviour—
is physically or sexually abusive; or
is emotionally or psychologically abusive; or
is economically abusive; or
is threatening; or
is coercive; or
in any other way controls or dominates the family member and causes that family member to feel fear for the safety or wellbeing of that family member or another person; or
behaviour by a person that causes a child to hear or witness, or otherwise be exposed to the effects of, behaviour referred to in paragraph (a).

history.raw: Examples to s. 5(1)(b) amended by No. 33/2018 s. 15.

nodes.text: Without limiting subsection (1), family violence includes the following behaviour—
assaulting or causing personal injury to a family member or threatening to do so;
sexually assaulting a family member or engaging in another form of sexually coercive behaviour or threatening to engage in such behaviour;
choking, strangling or suffocating (within the meaning of section 34AB(1) of the Crimes Act 1958) a family member or threatening to do so;
stalking a family member;
intentionally damaging a family member's property, or threatening to do so;
unlawfully depriving a family member of the family member's liberty, or threatening to do so;
using or misusing, or attempting or threatening to use or misuse, systems, processes and providers of services as a means of coercing or controlling a family member;

1. Intentional misuse of court processes for the purpose of coercing or controlling a family member. 2. Making malicious allegations or reports about the family member to entities such as Victoria Police, child protection services, health services, family services, and entities having responsibility for immigration.
influencing or attempting to influence the actions or decisions of providers of family, health and other services as a means of coercing or controlling a family member;

causing or threatening to cause the death or mistreatment of, or injury to, an animal, whether or not the animal belongs to the family member to whom the behaviour is directed so as to control, dominate or coerce the family member;
Mistreatment of an animal may include withholding the animal's food, water, shelter or medication.

causing or threatening to cause the sale, removal, abandonment, rehoming or surrendering of an animal, whether or not the animal belongs to the family member to whom the behaviour is directed so as to control, dominate or coerce the family member.
To remove doubt, it is declared that behaviour may constitute family violence even if the behaviour would not constitute a criminal offence.

nodes.heading: Meaning of economic abuse
nodes.text: For the purposes of this Act, economic abuse is behaviour by a person (the first person) that is coercive, deceptive or unreasonably controls another person (the second person), without the second person's consent—
in a way that denies the second person the economic or financial autonomy the second person would have had but for that behaviour; or

by withholding or threatening to withhold the financial support necessary for meeting the reasonable living expenses of the second person or the second person's child, if the second person is entirely or predominantly dependent on the first person for financial support to meet those living expenses. nodes.text: For the purposes of this Act, a family member, in relation to a person (a relevant person), means—
a person who is, or has been, the relevant person's spouse or domestic partner; or
a person who has, or has had, an intimate personal relationship with the relevant person; or
a person who is, or has been, a relative of the relevant person; or
a child who normally or regularly resides with the relevant person or has previously resided with the relevant person on a normal or regular basis; or
a child of a person who has, or has had, an intimate personal relationship with the relevant person.
For the purposes of subsections (1)(b) and (1)(e), a relationship may be an intimate personal relationship whether or not it is sexual in nature.

For the purposes of this Act, a family member of a person (the relevant person) also includes any other person whom the relevant person regards or regarded as being like a family member if it is or was reasonable to regard the other person as being like a family member having regard to the circumstances of the relationship, including the following—
the nature of the social and emotional ties between the relevant person and the other person;
whether the relevant person and the other person live together or relate together in a home environment;
the reputation of the relationship as being like family in the relevant person's and the other person's community;
the cultural recognition of the relationship as being like family in the relevant person's or other person's community;
the duration of the relationship between the relevant person and the other person and the frequency of contact;
any financial dependence or interdependence between the relevant person or other person;
any other form of dependence or interdependence between the relevant person and the other person;
the provision of any responsibility or care, whether paid or unpaid, between the relevant person and the other person;
the provision of sustenance or support between the relevant person and the other person.
A relationship between a person with a disability and the person's carer may over time have come to approximate the type of relationship that would exist between family members.
For the purposes of subsection (3), in deciding whether a person is a family member of a relevant person the relationship between the persons must be considered in its entirety.
For the purposes of this Act, domestic partner of a person means—
a person who is in a registered relationship within the meaning of the Relationships Act 2008 with the person; or

an adult to whom the person is not married but with whom the person is in a relationship as a couple where one or each of the persons provides personal or financial commitment and support of a domestic nature for the support of the other person.
For the purposes of subsection (1)(b), the following is irrelevant—
the genders of the persons;
whether or not the persons are living under the same roof.
Also, for the purposes of subsection (1)(b), a person is not the domestic partner of another person—
if the person provides domestic support and personal care to the person—
for fee or reward; or
on behalf of another person or an organisation, including a government or non-government agency, a body corporate or a charitable or benevolent organisation; or
merely because they are co-tenants.

In deciding whether persons who are not in a registered relationship are domestic partners of each other, all the circumstances of their relationship are to be taken into account, including any one or more of the matters referred to in section 35(2) of the Relationships Act 2008 as may be relevant in a particular case.
For the purposes of this Act, a relative of a person—
means any of the following, whether of the whole blood or half-blood or by marriage, and whether or not the relationship depends on adoption of the person—
the person's father, mother, grandfather or grandmother;
the person's son, daughter, grandson or granddaughter;
the person's brother or sister;
the person's uncle or aunt;
the person's nephew or niece;
the person's cousin; and
for an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander person—includes a person who, under Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander tradition or contemporary social practice, is the person's relative.
For domestic partners, a relative includes a person who would be a relative if the domestic partners were married to each other.

nodes.heading: Meaning of family violence intervention order, final order and interim order

nodes.text: For the purposes of this Act, a family violence intervention order means—
a final order referred to in subsection (2); or

For the purposes of this Act, a final order is an order made under section 74, 76, 77, 77A or 77B and includes—

an order made under section 74, 76, 77, 77A or 77B and confirmed on appeal to the County Court or Supreme Court.
For the purposes of this Act, an interim order is an order—
made under section 53, 53AA or 53AB, including  an order made under section 53, 53AA or 53AB as varied under section 100; and
made under section 60B or 60C, including an order made under section 60B or 60C as varied under section 100; and
made under section 101 that varies a family violence intervention order.

nodes.heading: Definitions
nodes.text: In this Division—

nodes.heading: directed person
nodes.text: means a person who is given a direction under section 14;

nodes.heading: police gaol
nodes.text: has the meaning given in the Corrections Act 1986.
Subject to subsection (2), a police officer may exercise a power under this Division in relation to a person if the police officer—
intends to make an application for one of the following against the person—
a family violence intervention order;
an order varying a family violence intervention order;
a family violence safety notice; or

reasonably believes that a family violence intervention order has been made or family violence safety notice has been issued against the person but not served, and the police officer intends to serve a copy of the order or notice on the person.
The police officer must not exercise the power unless—
the officer has reasonable grounds for suspecting that the person is an adult; and
the officer believes on reasonable grounds that exercise of the power is necessary to ensure the safety of a family member of the person or to preserve any property of the family member.

nodes.heading: Criteria for exercise of powers—recognised DVOs

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (2), a police officer may exercise a power under this Division in relation to a person if the police officer—
intends to make an application against the person for an order varying a recognised DVO; or
reasonably believes that the person is a respondent to a recognised DVO and the police officer—
intends to obtain a copy of the recognised DVO; and
if the recognised DVO has not been served, serve a copy on the person.
The police officer must not exercise the power unless—
the officer has reasonable grounds for suspecting that the person is an adult; and
the officer believes on reasonable grounds that exercise of the power is necessary to ensure the safety of a family member of the person or to preserve any property of the family member.
The police officer may direct the person, orally or in writing—
to remain at the place where the person is when the direction is given; or
to go to, and remain at, a place stated by the officer; or
to remain in the company of—
the officer; or
another police officer stated in the direction; or
another person (the accompanying person) stated by the officer.
A direction referred to in subsection (1)(c)(iii) may be given only with the accompanying person's consent.
A direction given under this section must be reasonable in the circumstances.
The directing officer must, at the time of giving the direction, inform the directed person, orally or in writing—
that the directed person may be apprehended and detained if the person refuses or fails to comply with the direction; and
that, if the directed person is apprehended and detained, it is an offence to escape or attempt to escape.
If a directed person refuses or fails to comply with a direction under section 14, a police officer may, using the force that is reasonably necessary, apprehend and detain the directed person.

The directed person may be detained at a police station or other place, but may be detained in a police gaol only if the officer considers it necessary to do so for the protection of any person or property, or to prevent the person from escaping from detention.
Section 49E of the Summary Offences Act 1966 makes it an offence to escape or attempt to escape from a place where a person is being lawfully detained.
Nothing in section 479C of the Crimes Act 1958 applies to a person who escapes or attempts to escape from detention under this Division.

nodes.heading: Search of person and seizure of objects

nodes.text: This section applies if a police officer gives a person a direction, or apprehends and detains a person, under this Division.

A police officer may search the person and any vehicle, package or thing in the person's possession if the officer suspects, on reasonable grounds, that the person has in the person's possession any object that may cause injury or damage or may be used to escape.
If the police officer finds any object that may cause injury or damage or may be used to escape, the police officer may—
if the object is a firearm, weapon or ammunition, issue a direction under section 158; or
in the case of any other object, seize the object.

An object seized under subsection (2A)(b) must be returned to the person when the direction ends or, if the person is detained, the authorisation for detention ends, unless the object is required as evidence in further proceedings under this Act or another Act.

To remove doubt, for the purposes of subsection (2) a suspicion that searching the person or any vehicle, package or thing in the person's possession would provide evidence that an offence has been or is being committed is not by itself sufficient grounds for conducting the search.

nodes.heading: Procedural requirements for person directed to a police station, or person apprehended and detained

history.raw: S. 17(8) inserted by No. 30/2010 s. 81, repealed by No. 48/2011 s. 27(1).

nodes.text: This section applies if—
a person is directed under section 14 to remain at, or go to and remain at, a police station; or
a directed person is apprehended and detained under section 15.
A police officer must—
inform the person that the person—
may communicate or attempt to communicate with a friend or relative (other than the affected family member or protected person) to inform the friend or relative of the person's whereabouts; and
may communicate or attempt to communicate with a legal practitioner; and
give the person a notice containing the prescribed information about the person's rights and responsibilities under this Division.
A police officer must comply with subsection (2)—
for a person referred to in subsection (1)(a)—as soon as practicable after—
the direction is given, if the person is at a police station when the direction is given; or
the person arrives at the police station, in any other case; and
for a person referred to in subsection (1)(b)—as soon as practicable after the person is apprehended and detained.
If the person wishes to communicate with a friend, relative or legal practitioner, a police officer must—
afford the person reasonable facilities as soon as practicable to enable the person to do so; and
allow the person's legal practitioner or a clerk of the legal practitioner to communicate with the person in circumstances in which, as far as practicable, the communication will not be overheard.
Nothing in subsection (4) permits the person to communicate with the affected family member or protected person.

If the person does not have sufficient knowledge of the English language to enable the person to understand why the person is subject to a direction or detention, a police officer must arrange for the person to have access to a competent interpreter.

Despite subsection (2) or (4), a police officer is not required to inform a person that the person may communicate or attempt to communicate with a friend or relative, or to afford a person facilities to enable the person to do so, if the officer believes on reasonable grounds that the communication would be likely to jeopardise the safety of the affected family member or protected person or any property of the affected family member or of the protected person.

If the person is subject to a residence restriction or exclusion condition, a place or area exclusion condition or a curfew condition attached to a community correction order under the Sentencing Act 1991 a police officer must notify the Secretary as soon as practicable that the person has been directed or apprehended and detained under this Act.

history.raw: S. 17(7A) inserted by No. 65/2011 s. 93, amended by No. 48/2018 s. 58(1).

nodes.text: In subsection (7A), curfew condition, place or area exclusion condition and residence restriction or exclusion condition have the same meaning as in the Sentencing Act 1991.

history.raw: S. 17(7B) inserted by No. 65/2011 s. 93, substituted by No. 48/2018 s. 58(2).

nodes.text: The maximum period for which a direction under this Division remains in force or a directed person may be detained under this Division is—
6 hours after the direction is given; or
if an extension is granted under section 19— that period as extended.

Despite subsection (1), in the case of a direction given for the reason in section 13(1)(a) or section 13A(1)(a), the direction ends and, if a directed person is detained under this Division, authorisation for the detention ends—

if a family violence intervention order is made or a recognised DVO is varied or a family violence safety notice is issued in respect of the directed person—at the time the order or notice is served on the directed person; or
if a warrant is issued under section 50 to arrest the directed person—at the time the directed person is arrested under the warrant; or

if a police officer decides not to make an application, or withdraws an application, for a family violence intervention order or a variation of a recognised DVO or family violence safety notice against the directed person—at the time of the decision or withdrawal.

Despite subsection (1), in the case of a direction given for the reason in section 13(1)(b), the direction ends and, if a directed person is detained under this Division, authorisation for the detention ends—
if the family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order is served on the directed person—at the time the order or notice is served on the directed person; or
if a police officer becomes aware that a family violence safety notice or family violence intervention order has not been made against the directed person.

Despite subsection (1), in the case of a direction given for the reason in section 13A(1)(b), the direction ends and, if a directed person is detained under this Division, authorisation for the detention ends—
if a police officer obtains a copy of the recognised DVO and that DVO has not been served—at the time the copy of the DVO is served on the directed person; or
if a police officer obtains a copy of the recognised DVO and that DVO has been served—at the time the copy of the recognised DVO is obtained; or
in any case, if a police officer becomes aware that the directed person is not a respondent to a recognised DVO.

If, despite a family violence intervention order or a family violence safety notice or recognised DVO being served on a directed person, or a copy of the recognised DVO being obtained, a police officer believes on reasonable grounds that it is necessary for the direction (and, if applicable, detention) to continue to enable further measures to be taken for the protection of the affected family member or protected person, the direction continues in force and detention (if applicable) is authorised until those measures have been taken or the period referred to in subsection (1) expires, whichever occurs first.

Sections 13 and 13A also require the police officer to believe on reasonable grounds that the continued direction or detention is necessary to ensure the safety of, or preserve any property of, the affected family member or protected person.

history.raw: Note to s. 18(3) substituted by No. 53/2016 s. 85(4), amended by No. 53/2016 s. 43(4).

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (5), the direction ends if an application for—
a family violence intervention order is refused in respect of the directed person; or
a family violence safety notice is refused in respect of the directed person; or
a warrant under section 50 to arrest a directed person is refused.

If a family violence safety notice or a warrant under section 50 to arrest a directed person is refused but the application for the family violence intervention order has not been withdrawn and the court has not yet determined whether an interim order is necessary or the application for the family violence order has not yet been made but is intended to be made by a police officer, the direction continues in force and detention (if applicable) is authorised until the direction ends under subsection (1), (2), (3) or (4)(a) (as the case may be).

Sections 13 and 13A also require the police officer to believe on reasonable grounds that the continued direction or detention is necessary to ensure the safety of, or preserve any property of, the affected family member or protected person.

history.raw: Note to s. 18(5) substituted by No. 53/2016 s. 85(5), amended by No. 53/2016 s. 43(5).

nodes.text: If a police officer considers it is necessary for a direction or the detention of a directed person under this Division to exceed 6 hours, the officer may apply to the court for an order extending the maximum period of the direction and, if applicable, detention.
An application for an extension order must—
be made within 6 hours after the direction was given to the directed person; and
include any prescribed particulars.

If the court is satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances, the court may make an order extending the maximum period of the direction and, if applicable, detention for a further period specified in the order.
The further period specified under subsection (3) must be a period expiring on or before the expiry of 10 hours after the direction was given to the directed person.
If an order is made under this section, a police officer must serve a copy of the order on the directed person.
This section does not apply if the direction is in relation to an application for a family violence safety notice.

nodes.heading: Telephone or fax application for extension order

nodes.text: A police officer may apply for an order under section 19 by telephone, fax or other electronic communication if—
the application is made—
before 9 a.m. or after 5 p.m. on a weekday; or
on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday; or
the officer reasonably believes that it is impracticable to make the application in person.
Before applying by telephone, fax or other electronic communication, the officer must complete an application setting out—
the grounds on which the order is sought; and
any other prescribed particulars.
On an application made by telephone, fax or other electronic communication, the court is not bound by the rules of evidence.
Despite anything to the contrary in subsection (3), Part 3.10 of the Evidence Act 2008 applies in respect of an application made by telephone, fax or other electronic communication.

history.raw: S. 20(3A) inserted by No. 69/2009 s. 54(Sch. Pt 1 item 22.1).

nodes.text: If the court makes an order under section 19 on an application made by telephone, fax or other electronic communication, the court must inform the officer of the terms of the order, the period of operation of the order and, if applicable, the venue of the court for the first mention date for the application for the family violence intervention order.
If an order under section 19 is made on an application made by telephone, the officer who made the application must—

complete a form of order in the terms indicated by the court under subsection (4) and must write on it the name of the magistrate who constituted the court that made the order and the date on which and the time at which it was made; and
ensure that the form of order completed by the officer is received at the venue of the court nominated in the order—
before the hearing of the application for the family violence intervention order; or
otherwise, as soon as practicable.

nodes.heading: Police to notify directed person when direction ceases
nodes.text: When a direction under this Division ends, a police officer must—
immediately notify, orally or in writing, the directed person that the direction has ended; and
if the directed person is detained under this Division, immediately release the directed person from detention; and
take reasonable steps to notify, orally or in writing, the protected person or affected family member that the direction has ended.
While a direction is in force under this Division a police officer must not interview or question the directed person in relation to any offence or alleged offence.
Subsection (1) applies whether or not the directed person is in detention under this Division.

nodes.heading: Court may hear directed person or affected family member or protected person

nodes.text: The court may, if practicable, hear a directed person or an affected family member or protected person on the hearing of an application for a family violence intervention order against the directed person or an application for an extension order under section 19, including an application made in accordance with section 20.
Subsection (1) applies whether or not the directed person is in detention under this Division.

history.raw: Pt 8 Div. 2 (Heading and ss 169A– 169C) inserted by No. 77/2014 s. 20.

nodes.heading: Application for family violence safety notice
nodes.text: A police officer who responds in person to an incident involving family violence may apply to another police officer, who is of the rank of Sergeant or a higher rank, for a family violence safety notice if—
the police officer has reasonable grounds for suspecting the respondent is an adult; and
the police officer has no reasonable grounds for suspecting the respondent has a cognitive impairment; and

the police officer has no reasonable grounds for suspecting there is a Family Law Act order or child protection order in force that may be inconsistent with the proposed terms of the family violence safety notice, after making reasonable enquiries of the respondent, the affected family member and any other adults at the scene of the incident; and
the police officer believes on reasonable grounds there is no family violence intervention order in place between the affected family member and respondent; and

the police officer has no reasonable grounds for suspecting there is a community correction order under the Sentencing Act 1991 in force that may be inconsistent with the proposed terms of the family violence safety notice; and

history.raw: S. 24(da) inserted by No. 30/2010 s. 82, repealed by No. 48/2011 s. 27(2), new s. 24(da) inserted by No. 65/2011 s. 94.

nodes.text: the police officer believes on reasonable grounds that, until an application for a family violence intervention order can be decided by the court, a family violence safety notice is necessary—
to ensure the safety of the affected family member; or
to preserve any property of the affected family member; or
to protect a child who has been subjected to family violence committed by the respondent.

nodes.heading: How an application may be made
nodes.text: An application for a family violence safety notice may be made—
in person; or
by fax or telephone or other electronic communication.

nodes.heading: Decision about family violence safety notice

nodes.text: A police officer of the rank of Sergeant or a higher rank who receives an application for a family violence safety notice may issue a family violence safety notice if—
the police officer believes on reasonable grounds there is no family violence intervention order in place between the affected family member and respondent; and
the police officer believes on reasonable grounds that issuing the notice is necessary—
to ensure the safety of the affected family member; or
to preserve any property of the affected family member; or
to protect a child who has been subjected to family violence committed by the respondent.
Before making a decision under subsection (1), the police officer making the decision—
must hear the police officer responding to the incident; and
must be satisfied that the grounds on which the police officer responding to the incident formed an opinion about the matters referred to in section 24(a), (b), (c) and (d) are reasonable; and
may, if practicable, hear the respondent or the affected family member.

nodes.heading: Issue of family violence safety notice if recognised DVO in place

nodes.text: A police officer may issue a family violence safety notice for the protection of a person against a respondent whether or not there is a recognised DVO in relation to the same respondent and protected person.

If a police officer believes there may be a recognised DVO made by a court of any jurisdiction in relation to the same respondent and protected person, the police officer must before the first mention date, make reasonable enquiries to determine whether there is a recognised DVO in relation to the same respondent and protected person.

nodes.heading: Form of family violence safety notice

nodes.text: If a police officer issues a family violence safety notice under section 26 on an application made in person, the police officer must—
include in the notice matters referred to in section 32; and
make the notice on oath or by affirmation or by affidavit or certify the notice.

history.raw: S. 27(1)(b) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 52.1).

nodes.text: If a police officer issues a family violence safety notice on an application made by telephone, fax or other electronic communication, the police officer must—
complete a form (an authorisation form) that contains the following information—
the names of the respondent and protected person;
the name, rank and station of the police officer who made the application;
a brief statement of the reasons for issuing the family violence safety notice;
the conditions of the family violence safety notice; and
certify the authorisation form; and
inform the officer who made the application of the terms of the authorisation form referred to in paragraph (a)(iii) and (iv).
If a family violence safety notice is issued on an application made by telephone, fax or other electronic communication, the police officer who made the application must—
complete a form (a safety notice form) that includes the information referred to in section 32; and
certify the safety notice form.

nodes.heading: Procedure if safety notice form completed

nodes.text: This section applies if a family violence safety notice is issued on an application made by telephone, fax or other electronic communication and a safety notice form is completed.
As soon as practicable after the issue of the family violence safety notice a police officer of the rank of Sergeant or a higher rank must—
check the authorisation form and safety notice form to ensure the forms are consistent; and

if there are any material discrepancies between the forms, correct the safety notice form to ensure it accurately reflects the conditions included in the authorisation form and sufficiently identifies the respondent and protected person; and
certify the safety notice form as being consistent with the authorisation form, as corrected under paragraph (b) if necessary.
See section 34 which provides for the service of the corrected notice and the filing of the corrected notice with the Magistrates' Court.
For the purposes of subsection (2), there is a material discrepancy between an authorisation form and a safety notice form if—
the safety notice form omits a condition included in the authorisation form; or
the safety notice form includes an additional condition to the conditions included in the authorisation form; or

the safety notice form changes the scope of a condition in the authorisation form so that it requires the respondent to do something or refrain from doing something that is not set out in the authorisation form; or
the respondent named in the safety notice form is not the respondent named in the authorisation form; or
the protected person named in the safety notice form is not the protected person named in the authorisation form.

Also, for the purposes of subsection (2)(b), if there is a material discrepancy between the safety notice form and the authorisation form, the safety notice form is invalid to the extent of the material discrepancy until a corrected safety notice form is served on the respondent under section 34.

nodes.heading: Conditions of family violence safety notice

nodes.text: A family violence safety notice may include any condition the court may include under section 81(2)(a) to (f) in a family violence intervention order.

Before including in a family violence safety notice a condition prohibiting the respondent from being anywhere within a specified distance from a particular place, the police officer issuing the notice must make reasonable enquiries to ensure this will be practical in the particular circumstances.

nodes.heading: Duration of family violence safety notice

nodes.text: A family violence safety notice—
starts when the notice or a safety notice form is served on the respondent; and
subject to subsection (1A), ends when the earlier of the following occurs—

the court adjourns the application for the family violence intervention order or refuses to make a family violence intervention order on the first mention date for the application for the family violence intervention order;
if the court makes a family violence intervention order on the first mention date—the order is served on the respondent.

If, at the time the family violence safety notice was issued, there was a recognised DVO made by a court of any jurisdiction in relation to the same respondent and protected person, the family violence safety notice ends when the earlier of the following occurs—
on the first mention date, if the application for the family violence intervention order is withdrawn on the first mention date;
if the court varies or extends the recognised DVO on the first mention date— when the order is served on the respondent.
To avoid doubt, it is declared that if a safety notice form is subsequently corrected and served on the respondent under section 34(b)—
the family violence safety notice is taken to have started when a safety notice form referred to in subsection (1)(a) was served on the respondent; and
the time by which the first mention date must be held, as referred to in section 31(3)(a), must be measured from the service of that form.

nodes.heading: Family violence safety notice taken to be application for family violence intervention order

nodes.text: A family violence safety notice is taken to be—
an application by the police officer who applied for it for a family violence intervention order for the protected person against the respondent; and
a summons for the respondent to attend at the first mention date for the application stated in the notice.

history.raw: S. 31(1)(b) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 57.1).

nodes.text: A family violence safety notice that has ended under section 30(1)(b) continues to be taken to be an application for a family violence intervention order until the court finally determines the application or the application is withdrawn.
A family violence safety notice must be returned to the court at the first mention date stated in the notice.
The first mention date for the application must be—

history.raw: S. 31(3) amended by No. 83/2012 s. 4, substituted by No. 77/2014 s. 6.

nodes.text: as soon as practicable if—
the family violence safety notice includes an exclusion condition that excludes the respondent from the respondent's primary place of residence; and
the police officer who applied for the family violence safety notice believes that the respondent may not have access to temporary accommodation; and
in any case, not later than 14 days after the family violence safety notice or form of notice completed under section 27(3) is served.

nodes.heading: Information to be included in family violence safety notice
nodes.text: The following information must be included in a family violence safety notice—
the names of the respondent and the protected person;
the time and date the notice was issued;
the time, date and location for the first mention date for an application for a family violence intervention order relating to the incident;
that the notice is a summons for the respondent to attend at the court on the first mention date;

history.raw: S. 32(d) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 57.2).

nodes.text: the period for which the notice applies;
a brief statement of the reasons for issuing the notice, including information addressing the grounds for issuing the notice referred to in section 26;
the conditions of the notice;
an address nominated by the respondent for service of documents, if provided;
the name, rank and station of the police officer issuing the notice;
the name, rank and station of the police officer who applied for the notice;
any other matters prescribed.
If a police officer issues a family violence safety notice, that police officer, or the police officer who applied for the notice, must—
ask the respondent to provide an address for the service of documents; and
advise the respondent that a police officer may, under section 207, seek information about the respondent from public sector organisations—
to enable a police officer to locate the respondent and serve the respondent with a document under this Act; or
to enable the respondent to be served with a document under an order for alternative service.
Without limiting subsection (1), the address may be—
the address of accommodation arranged under section 36; or
the address of a friend or family member of the respondent; or
an email address.
The family violence safety notice must be served on the respondent personally. See section 202(2).

history.raw: Notes to s. 33(2) inserted by No. 19/2017 s. 25(2)(b).

nodes.text: Other documents may be served by email if the court makes an order for alternative service. See section 202A.
The respondent is not obliged to comply with the request to provide an address.

If the respondent provides an address under subsection (1) other than the address where the respondent lives or works and another person living at the address advises the court that the person does not consent to the use of the address for the service of documents under this Act, the address is not a valid address for the service of the documents.

nodes.heading: Service of family violence safety notice
nodes.text: As soon as practicable after a family violence safety notice is issued, a police officer must—
serve a copy of the family violence safety notice on the respondent and the protected person; and

if the family violence safety notice is a safety notice form that has been subsequently corrected under section 28, serve a copy of the corrected safety notice form on the respondent and the protected person; and
file with the Magistrates' Court—
if the family violence safety notice was issued on an application made under section 25(a), a copy of the form completed under section 27(1); or
if the family violence safety notice was issued on an application made under section 25(b), a copy of the safety notice form certified under section 28(2)(c).

nodes.heading: Explanation of family violence safety notice

nodes.text: A police officer who serves a family violence safety notice on a respondent or a protected person must—
explain the notice to the respondent or protected person; and
take reasonable steps to ensure the respondent or protected person understands the nature and consequences of the notice.
Without limiting subsection (1), the police officer who serves a notice on a respondent or gives a copy of the notice to the protected person must explain—
the purpose of the notice; and
the duration of the notice; and
the conditions of the notice; and
the consequences of the respondent contravening the notice; and
that the notice may be enforced against the respondent in another State or a Territory under the National Domestic Violence Order Scheme Act 2016 and corresponding DVO recognition laws; and
that the protected person cannot consent to the respondent contravening the notice; and
that the notice is a summons to attend court on the first mention date specified in the notice and the consequences for failing to attend court at that time on that date; and
the right of the respondent or protected person to obtain legal advice before the first mention date; and
any other matter prescribed under the regulations.

If the police officer determines that the respondent or protected person is unable to sufficiently understand the English language, the officer must comply with the officer's obligations under this section via a competent interpreter.
Failure by a police officer to comply with this section does not invalidate a family violence safety notice.
If a police officer serves a family violence safety notice on a respondent that  includes an exclusion condition, the officer must—
consider the accommodation needs of the respondent and any dependent children of the respondent; and
take any reasonable steps necessary to ensure the respondent and any dependent children of the respondent have access to temporary accommodation.
If a police officer serves a family violence safety notice on a respondent and the notice does not include an exclusion condition, the police officer must—
consider the accommodation needs of the protected person and any dependent children of the protected person; and
take any reasonable steps necessary to ensure the protected person and any dependent children have access to temporary accommodation.

To avoid any doubt, the requirement under subsection (1)(b) or (2)(b) does not include an obligation for the police officer to provide free accommodation for the respondent, the protected person or the dependent children of either the respondent or protected person.

nodes.heading: Contravention of family violence safety notice

nodes.text: This section applies if a person—
has been served with a family violence safety notice; and
has had an explanation of the notice given to the person in accordance with section 35.
The person must not contravene the notice.
Penalty: Level 7 imprisonment (2 years maximum) or a level 7 fine (240 penalty units maximum) or both.

It is immaterial that some or all of the course of conduct constituting an offence against subsection (2) occurred outside Victoria, so long as the protected person was in Victoria at the time at which that conduct occurred.

It is immaterial that the protected person was outside Victoria at the time at which some or all of the course of conduct constituting an offence against subsection (2) occurred, so long as that conduct occurred in Victoria.
In a proceeding for an offence against subsection (2) constituted by contravening a family violence safety notice, it is a defence to the charge for the accused person to prove that—
the accused person was the respondent under the family violence safety notice; and
a family violence intervention order in relation to the same protected person and respondent was also in force at the time the offence was alleged to have been committed; and
the accused person's conduct was not in contravention of the family violence intervention order.
In a proceeding for an offence against subsection (2), it is not a defence to the charge that—
the accused person was the respondent under the family violence safety notice; and
a recognised DVO in relation to the same protected person and respondent—
was made before the family violence safety notice was issued; and
was in force at the time the offence was alleged to have been committed; and
the accused person's conduct was not a contravention of the recognised DVO.

nodes.heading: Contravention of notice intending to cause harm or fear for safety

nodes.text: In this section—

nodes.heading: mental harm
nodes.text: includes—
psychological harm; and
suicidal thoughts.
A person who—
has been served with a family violence safety notice; and
has had an explanation of the notice given to him or her in accordance with section 35—
must not contravene the notice intending to cause, or knowing that his or her conduct will probably cause—
physical or mental harm to the protected person, including self-harm; or
apprehension or fear in the protected person for his or her own safety or that of any other person.
Penalty: Level 6 imprisonment (5 years maximum) or a level 6 fine (600 penalty units maximum) or both.

It is immaterial that some or all of the course of conduct constituting an offence against subsection (2) occurred outside Victoria, so long as the protected person was in Victoria at the time at which that conduct occurred.

It is immaterial that the protected person was outside Victoria at the time at which some or all of the course of conduct constituting an offence against subsection (2) occurred, so long as that conduct occurred in Victoria.
In a proceeding for an offence against subsection (2), it is a defence to the charge for the accused person to prove that—
the accused person was the respondent under the family violence safety notice; and
a family violence intervention order in relation to the same protected person and respondent was also in force at the time the offence was alleged to have been committed; and
the accused person's conduct was not in contravention of the family violence intervention order.
In a proceeding for an offence against subsection (2), it is not a defence to the charge that—
the accused person was the respondent under the family violence safety notice; and
a recognised DVO in relation to the same protected person and respondent—
was made before the family violence safety notice was issued; and
was in force at the time the offence was alleged to have been committed; and
the accused person's conduct was not in contravention of the recognised DVO.

nodes.heading: Arrest for contravention of family violence safety notice
nodes.text: If a police officer believes on reasonable grounds that a person has committed an offence against section 37, the officer may, without warrant, arrest and detain the person.
Section 459(1) of the Crimes Act 1958 provides for apprehension without warrant of a person reasonably believed to have committed an indictable offence.

history.raw: Note to s. 38 inserted by No. 83/2012 s. 7.

nodes.heading: Family violence intervention order prevails over family violence safety notice

nodes.text: This section applies if—
a police officer issues a family violence safety notice; and
there is an existing family violence intervention order in place between the affected family member and respondent.
To the extent of any inconsistency between the family violence safety notice and the family violence intervention order, the family violence intervention order prevails.

nodes.heading: Family violence safety notice prevails over existing recognised DVO

history.raw: S. 40 repealed by No. 77/2013 s. 24, new s. 40 inserted by No. 53/2016 s. 49.

nodes.text: This section applies if—
a police officer issues a family violence safety notice in relation to a respondent and protected person; and
at the time the family violence safety notice is issued, there is a recognised DVO made by a court in relation to the same respondent and protected person.
Subject to subsection (3), the respondent must comply with both the family violence safety notice and the recognised DVO as it operates in Victoria.

If it is not possible for the respondent to comply with the family violence safety notice and the recognised DVO as it operates in Victoria at the same time, the respondent must comply with the family violence safety notice.

nodes.heading: Application for family violence intervention order
Where application for family violence intervention order may be made
nodes.text: An application for a family violence intervention order must be made at the proper venue of the Magistrates' Court or Children's Court.

nodes.heading: How application is to be made

nodes.text: An application for a family violence intervention order must—
include the information prescribed by rules made under this Act; and
if the applicant is a police officer, be made on oath or by affirmation or by affidavit or certified in accordance with subsection (2); or

history.raw: S. 43(1)(b) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 52.1).

nodes.text: if the applicant is not a police officer, be made on oath or by affirmation or by affidavit or by declaration of truth.
For the purposes of subsection (1)(b), an application certified by a police officer must—
be signed by the police officer; and
include the police officer's name, rank and station.
Unless the rules of court otherwise provide, the application may be made by telephone, fax or other electronic communication.
A declaration of truth—
must include the applicant's full name and date of birth; and
must include an acknowledgment that the content of the application is true and correct to the best of the applicant's knowledge and belief; and

must include an acknowledgment that the applicant knows that making a declaration of truth that the applicant knows to be false is an offence with a penalty of 600 penalty units or 5 years imprisonment or both; and
must otherwise comply with any requirements of the rules of court (if any); and
is not required to be witnessed by, or executed before, any other person.

nodes.heading: Who may apply for family violence intervention order
nodes.text: An application for a family violence intervention order may be made by—
a police officer; or
However, see section 75 which provides that a final order can be made without the consent of the affected family member but only with limited conditions.
an affected family member; or
if the affected family member is an adult, any other person with the written consent of the affected family member; or
if the affected family member is a child—
a parent of the child; or
any other person with the written consent of a parent of the child or with the leave of the court; or
the affected family member with the leave of the court if the affected family member is of or above the age of 14 years; or
if the affected family member has a guardian—
the guardian; or
any other person, with the leave of the court.
See also section 76(4) which provides that an associate of an affected family member or a protected person may apply for a family violence intervention order.
If an application for leave is made under section 45(d)(ii) or (e)(ii), the court must grant leave if it is satisfied that it is in the best interests of the affected family member to do so.

If an application for leave is made under section 45(d)(iii), the court must not grant leave unless it is satisfied the child understands the nature and consequences of a family violence intervention order.

nodes.heading: Application for protection of child may be included in application for protection of child's parent

nodes.text: An application for a family violence intervention order for an affected family member who is a child may be included in an application for the protection of the child's parent if the applications arise out of the same or similar circumstances.

An application referred to in subsection (1) may, on the application of the applicant or the respondent, be heard separately if the court thinks fit having regard to any advantages of the matters being heard together.

nodes.heading: Service of application
nodes.text: As soon as practicable after an application for a family violence intervention order is made, the appropriate registrar for the court must serve the application on—
the respondent; and
if the applicant for the order is not the affected family member—
the affected family member; or
if the affected family member is a child and the application was made with the consent of the child's parent, that parent;
if the affected family member is a child and the application was made with the leave of the court, a parent of the child (other than the respondent) with whom the child normally or regularly lives;
if the affected family member has a guardian—the guardian.
See section 205(1), which provides that a person may serve a document by causing it to be served.

history.raw: Note to s. 48 inserted by No. 53/2010 s. 198.

nodes.heading: Registrar may issue summons on application for family violence intervention order
nodes.text: If an application for a family violence intervention order has been made to the court, the appropriate registrar for the court may issue a summons requiring the respondent to attend at the court for the hearing of the application.

nodes.heading: Magistrate or registrar may issue warrant on certain applications for family violence intervention orders

nodes.text: A magistrate or an appropriate registrar for the court may issue a warrant for the arrest of an adult respondent, as if the application for a family violence intervention order alleged the commission of an offence, if the magistrate or registrar believes on reasonable grounds it is necessary—
to ensure the safety of the affected family member; or
to preserve any property of the affected family member; or
to protect a child who has been subjected to family violence committed by the respondent; or
to ensure the respondent attends court at a mention date for the application.

If a warrant has been issued to arrest a respondent, a police officer may arrest the respondent although the execution copy of the warrant is not in the police officer's possession at the time of the arrest.

In determining whether it is necessary to issue a warrant under subsection (1), the magistrate or registrar is not to take into account whether or not the respondent is or has been the subject of a direction, or detained, under Division 1 of Part 3.

nodes.heading: Application by affidavit or certified if warrant to issue
nodes.text: If the applicant for a family violence intervention order seeks a warrant to issue in the first instance for the arrest of the respondent—

history.raw: S. 51 (Heading) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 52.2).

nodes.text: the application for the warrant must be in writing and be made by affidavit or be certified; and

history.raw: S. 51(a) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 52.3).

nodes.text: the application for the family violence intervention order and the warrant must be in the same document and contain the prescribed particulars.

The Bail Act 1977 applies to and in respect of a respondent to an application for a family violence intervention order arrested under a warrant as if the respondent were an accused person charged with an offence to whom section 4 of the Bail Act 1977 applies.
For the purposes of subsection (1), the appropriate person must—
advise the affected family member of the outcome of the application for bail; and
if bail is granted—
advise the affected family member of any conditions imposed on the respondent that are intended to protect the affected family member; and
give the affected family member a copy of the undertaking of bail.
In subsection (2)— appropriate person means—
if the application for bail is considered by a court (other than a bail justice), the appropriate registrar of the court; and
if the application for bail is considered by a bail justice or a police officer, the police officer.

nodes.heading: Court to consider any children before deciding on interim order
nodes.text: Before deciding whether to make an interim order under section 53, the court must consider whether there are any children who have been subjected to family violence committed by the respondent.

history.raw: S. 53(1A)(1B) inserted by No. 18/2010 s. 18(2), repealed by No. 19/2017 s. 6(2).

nodes.text: The court may make an interim order if—

a person has applied to the court for a family violence intervention order and the court is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that an interim order is necessary pending a final decision about the application—
to ensure the safety of the affected family member; or
to preserve any property of the affected family member; or
to protect an affected family member who is a child who has been subjected to family violence committed by the respondent; or

history.raw: S. 53(1)(a)(iii) amended by No. 18/2010 s. 18(1), substituted by No. 19/2017 s. 6(1).

nodes.text: a person has applied to the court for a family violence intervention order and the parties to the proceeding have consented to, or do not oppose, the making of an interim order for the application; or

a family violence safety notice has been issued for an affected family member and the court is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, there are no circumstances that would justify discontinuing the protection of the person until a final decision about the application.

See Division 5 which provides for the inclusion of conditions in a family violence intervention order, including an interim order.  See also Division 5 which provides for the inclusion of conditions suspending a firearms authority, weapons approval or weapons exemption in the case of an interim order and cancelling a firearms authority, weapons approval or weapons exemption in the case of a final order.

history.raw: Note to s. 53(1) amended by No. 53/2010 s. 200(1).

nodes.text: The court may make an order under subsection (1)(b)—
without being satisfied as to any matter referred to in subsection (1)(a) or (1)(c); and
whether or not the respondent admits to any or all of the particulars of the application.
In deciding whether to make an interim order the court is not to take into account whether or not the respondent is or has been the subject of a direction, or detained, under Division 1 of Part 3.
The court may make an interim order whether or not—

history.raw: S. 53(3) inserted by No. 53/2010 s. 200(2), substituted by No. 1/2026 s. 16.

nodes.text: some or all of the alleged family violence occurred outside Victoria; and
the affected family member was outside Victoria at the time at which some or all of the family violence alleged in the application for the family violence intervention order occurred.
The application for the family violence intervention order must be made to the proper venue of the court—see section 42.

The court may make an interim order at any time after the making of an application for a family violence intervention order and before the final decision about the application is made, and may do so whether or not the court has previously made or refused to make an interim order.

nodes.heading: Court must make interim order for a child if court makes interim order for affected family member

nodes.text: This section applies if—
the court makes an interim order under section 53(1) in relation to an affected family member; and
the court is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that a child has been subjected to family violence committed by the respondent (whether or not that child is also an affected family member).
If the court makes the interim order under section 53(1)(a) or (c), subject to subsection (4), the court must—
if the child's need for protection is substantially the same as that of the affected family member, include the child in the interim order as a protected person; or
otherwise, make a separate interim order for the child as a protected person.

If the court makes the interim order by consent under section 53(1)(b), and that order does not include the child, subject to subsection (4), the court must make a separate interim order for the child as a protected person.

The court is not required to include the child in the interim order or to make a separate interim order to protect the child if the court is satisfied that it is not necessary to do so to protect the child or ensure the safety of the child pending a final decision about the application.

nodes.heading: Interim protection of child on court's own initiative—interim order not made for affected family member

history.raw: S. 53AB inserted by No. 19/2017 s. 7, amended by No. 33/2018 s. 19 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text: If the court does not make an interim order under section 53(1) in relation to an affected family member, the court may, on its own initiative, make an interim order for a child as a protected person if satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that—
the child has been subjected to family violence committed by the respondent; and
an interim order is necessary to protect the child pending a final decision about the application.
An interim order under subsection (1) is an order in the proceeding under section 53 and, for the purposes of any proceeding for any final order under section 74 or 76—
the applicant for the final order is—
the affected family member who made the initial application referred to in section 53(1); or
if the affected family member did not make the application referred to in section 53(1), the person who made that application on behalf of the affected family member; or
if neither subparagraph (i) or (ii) apply, in accordance with subsection (3), the Chief Commissioner of Police; and
the child is a party to the proceeding; and
the respondent to the initial application referred to in section 53(1) is a party to the proceeding; and
any application for the final order may be dealt with in accordance with this Act in the same way as any other application; and
the application for the final order in respect of the child is not affected by the initial application referred to in section 53(1) being struck out or withdrawn.
In making an interim order referred to in this section, the court may appoint the Chief Commissioner of Police to be the applicant for any final order in respect of the child if satisfied that—
the Chief Commissioner of Police is not a person referred to in subsection (2)(a)(ii); and
the appointment is necessary in all the circumstances, having regard to the child's safety.
If the court makes an appointment under subsection (3), the court must ensure that the Chief Commissioner of Police is given—
a copy of the interim order which makes that appointment; and
a copy of the application referred to in section 53(1).
See also section 152.

nodes.heading: Interim family violence intervention order where existing personal safety intervention order

nodes.text: The court must not make an interim order if there is an existing personal safety intervention order for which—
the affected family member is a protected person and the respondent is a respondent; or
the respondent is a protected person and the affected family member is a respondent.

Despite subsection (1), the court may make an interim order if there is an existing interim personal safety intervention order for which the affected family member is a respondent and the respondent is a protected person.

B is an affected family member for an application for a family violence intervention order against A.  However, A is already a protected person under an interim personal safety intervention order, and B is a respondent for that order. The court could still make an interim order to protect B from A.
In this section, interim personal safety intervention order means an interim order within the meaning of the Personal Safety Intervention Orders Act 2010.

nodes.heading: Interim order may be made in absence of respondent etc.
nodes.text: An interim order may be made—
whether or not the respondent has been served with a copy of the application for a family violence intervention order; and
whether or not the respondent is present when the interim order is made.

nodes.heading: Evidentiary requirements for making interim orders

nodes.text: The court must not make an interim order, other than an order referred to in section 53(1)(b), unless—
the application is supported by oral evidence or an affidavit; or
the court waives the requirement under paragraph (a); or
the application is made by the issue of a family violence safety notice that was certified in accordance with section 153(1).
The court may waive the requirement that the application be supported by oral evidence or an affidavit if—
the applicant is a police officer and the application is made by electronic communication—
provided that the court has considered whether it is practicable to obtain oral evidence or an affidavit before making the interim order; or
the application is made before 9 a.m. or after 5 p.m. on a weekday or on a Saturday, Sunday or a public holiday and the application was certified in accordance with section 43(2); or

the applicant is not a police officer and the application is made by a declaration of truth, provided that the court has considered whether it is practicable to obtain oral evidence or an affidavit before making the interim order.
Nothing in subsection (1)(a) or (3) obliges the affected family member to give evidence before the interim order is made.

If the application is made by issue of a family violence safety notice that was certified in accordance with section 153(1), the court, if deciding under section 65(3) whether to refuse to admit or limit the use to be made of the family violence safety notice, must first consider whether it is reasonably practicable to obtain oral evidence or affidavit evidence.

nodes.heading: Interim order may apply to more than one affected family member
nodes.text: An interim order may be made for more than one affected family member if—
the court is satisfied under section 53(1)(a) in relation to each of the affected family members; or
all the parties to the proceeding have given consent, or are not opposed to the making of the order, in accordance with section 53(1)(b); or
a family violence safety notice has been issued for each of the affected family members and the court is satisfied under section 53(1)(c) in relation to each of the family members.
This section applies if the court makes an interim order against a respondent who is an adult.

If the court makes an interim order, and the respondent or protected person (or both) are before the court, the court must explain to the respondent and protected person (or whichever of them is before the court) the following matters—
the purpose, terms and effect of the interim order;
the consequences and penalties that may follow if the respondent fails to comply with the terms of the interim order;
that the interim order may be enforced against the respondent in another State or a Territory under the National Domestic Violence Order Scheme Act 2016 and corresponding DVO recognition laws; and
when the interim order expires and the means by which the interim order may be varied;
for the respondent, that the interim order is a civil order of the court and the protected person cannot give permission to contravene the interim order;
the process for deciding the final order;
how the order interacts with a Family Law Act order or an order under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005;
if the court has varied, suspended, revoked or revived a Family Law Act order because it is inconsistent with the interim order, the purpose, terms and effect of the variation or suspension;
any relevant family violence services offering legal, emotional or practical support that may be available to the protected person or respondent.
An explanation under subsection (1) must be a clear oral explanation.
A written notice including the matters referred to in subsection (1), in the form prescribed by the rules, must—

history.raw: S. 57(2A) inserted by No. 18/2010 s. 20(2), substituted by No. 19/2017 s. 17(4).

nodes.text: be given to the protected person and respondent (or whichever of them is before the court) with a copy of the interim order; or
otherwise, be given to the protected person or be served on the respondent, with the copy of the interim order.
The written notice may include any additional information the court considers necessary to explain the interim order.
A failure by the court to explain an interim order in accordance with this section does not affect the validity of the interim order.
This section applies if the court makes an interim order against a respondent who is a child.

If the court makes an interim order, and the respondent or protected person (or both) are before the court, the court must explain to the respondent and protected person (or whichever of them is before the court) the following matters—
the purpose, terms and effect of the interim order;
the consequences and penalties that may follow if the respondent fails to comply with the terms of the interim order;
that the interim order may be enforced against the respondent in another State or a Territory under the National Domestic Violence Order Scheme Act 2016 and corresponding DVO recognition laws;
when the interim order expires and the means by which the interim order may be varied;
for the respondent, that the interim order is a civil order of the court and the protected person cannot give permission to contravene the interim order;
the process for deciding the final order;
how the order interacts with a Family Law Act order or an order under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005;
if the court has varied, suspended, revoked or revived a Family Law Act order because it is inconsistent with the interim order, the purpose, terms and effect of the variation or suspension;
any relevant family violence services offering legal, emotional or practical support that may be available to the protected person or respondent.
An explanation under subsection (2) must be a clear oral explanation.
A written notice including the matters referred to in subsection (2), in the form prescribed by the rules, must—
be served on the respondent with the copy of the interim order; and
be given to the protected person with the copy of the interim order.
The written notice may include any additional information the court considers necessary to explain the interim order.
A failure by the court to explain an interim order in accordance with this section does not affect the validity of the interim order.

nodes.heading: Interim order made on electronic application by police
nodes.text: If the court makes an order under section 53 on an application made by a police officer by telephone, fax or other electronic communication, the court must inform the police officer of—
the terms of the order; and
the period of operation of the order; and
the venue of the court for the first mention date for the application for the family violence intervention order; and
the date and time of the first mention date for the application for the family violence intervention order .
See section 5(2) of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 which provides that the Magistrates' Court may sit and act at any time and place.

nodes.heading: Hearing to be listed for decision about final order as soon as practicable
nodes.text: If the court makes an interim order, the court must ensure the hearing is listed for a decision about the final order as soon as practicable.

nodes.heading: Expiry of interim order
nodes.text: An interim order ends—

if the court makes a final order and the final order includes an order that the interim order continues until the final order is served on the respondent, when the final order is served on the respondent; or
if the court makes a final order and the final order does not include an order about the interim order continuing as referred to in paragraph (a), at the time the final order is made; or
if the court refuses to make a final order in relation to the application, at the time of the court's refusal; or
if the interim order is revoked by the court, at the time of the revocation; or
if the application for the family violence intervention order is withdrawn, at the time of the withdrawal.
See section 100 which provides for the variation of family violence intervention orders, including interim orders.

If, in making the interim order, the court also revives, varies or suspends an order, injunction or arrangement under section 68R of the Family Law Act 1975 of the Commonwealth, that revival, variation or suspension ceases to have effect under section 68T of that Act when the interim order ends or 21 days after the interim order is made, whichever is earlier.

nodes.heading: Interim orders made on court's own motion in bail proceeding or in criminal proceeding

history.raw: Pt 4 Div. 2A (Heading and ss 60A–60L) inserted by No. 33/2018 s. 22.

nodes.heading: Definitions for this Division
nodes.text: In this Division—

nodes.heading: application or appeal relating to bail
nodes.text: means any of the following under the Bail Act 1977—

path.definition: application or appeal relating to bail

history.raw: S. 60A def. of application or appeal relating to bail amended by No. 1/2026 s. 3(a).
history.def_name: application or appeal relating to bail

nodes.text: an application for bail;

path.definition: application or appeal relating to bail

nodes.text: an application to vary conditions of bail;

path.definition: application or appeal relating to bail

nodes.text: an application to extend bail;

path.definition: application or appeal relating to bail

nodes.text: an application to revoke bail;

path.definition: application or appeal relating to bail

nodes.text: an appeal under section 18A;

path.definition: application or appeal relating to bail

nodes.text: an appeal under section 18AG;

path.definition: application or appeal relating to bail

nodes.heading: relevant party
nodes.text: means, in a criminal proceeding, the party who—

history.raw: S. 60A def. of relevant party inserted by No. 1/2026 s. 3(b).

nodes.text: is accused; or
has been found guilty; or
is appealing having been found guilty; or
has had their finding of guilt set aside on appeal.

nodes.heading: Court hearing application or appeal relating to bail may make own motion interim order

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (3), a court hearing an application or appeal relating to bail may make an interim order against an accused to protect a family member of the accused if the court is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the interim order is necessary to ensure the safety of the family member pending a decision about a final order.
A court may make an interim order under this section on its own motion.
The court must not make an interim order to protect a family member of the accused if—
there is an existing family violence intervention order that protects that family member of the accused from the accused; or
an application for a family violence intervention order that protects that family member of the accused from the accused has been made but not finally determined.

nodes.heading: Court may make interim order on its own motion in a criminal proceeding

nodes.text: Subject to subsection (4), a court hearing a criminal proceeding may make an interim order against a relevant party to protect a family member of the relevant party if the court is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the interim order is necessary to ensure the safety of the family member pending a decision about a final order.
A court may make an interim order under this section on its own motion.
The court may make an interim order under subsection (1)—
at any stage of the criminal proceeding, including during any trial, any sentencing hearing or any appeal; and
whether or not the relevant party is found guilty of the offence; and
whether or not the charge is withdrawn or the prosecution of the offence is discontinued.
The court must not make an interim order to protect a family member of the relevant party if—
there is an existing family violence intervention order that protects that family member of the relevant party from the relevant party; or
an application for a family violence intervention order that protects that family member of the relevant party from the relevant party has been made but not finally determined.

nodes.heading: Prosecutor not party to proceeding for interim order

nodes.text: The prosecutor in any criminal proceeding in which an interim order is made or proposed to be made under this Division is not a party to the proceeding, and has no standing or status in the proceeding, only for the purposes of the making of the interim order.
Nothing in subsection (1) affects the status, function or standing of a prosecutor in relation to the criminal proceeding other than the making of the interim order.

nodes.heading: Material before the court for making interim orders under this Division

nodes.text: Nothing in Division 3 or 3A applies to the making of an interim order under section 60B or 60C.
An interim order under section 60B or 60C must be made on the material before the court in the hearing of the application or appeal relating to bail, or the criminal proceeding.
